analysis.one_liner: Makes members of Congress repay taxpayer money spent settling their own harassment and discrimination cases and overhauls how staff complaints are handled.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote one day after it was introduced, but the Senate never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Congressional Accountability Act, employees of Congress who allege harassment or discrimination had to go through mandatory counseling and mediation before filing a claim, and any settlements were paid from a Treasury account rather than by the member responsible. This bill removed those roadblocks, required current and former members to repay the Treasury for awards and settlements tied to their own conduct — with the money docked from their salary or retirement account if they didn't pay — and automatically sent member and senior-staff cases to the ethics committees. It also extended workplace-rights protections to unpaid interns, Library of Congress employees, and several commission staffs, and required public reporting of settlement payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 30,000 legislative branch employees, plus unpaid interns, fellows, and Library of Congress staff. They get a faster path to filing claims (no mandatory counseling or mediation first), an investigation with subpoena power, the option of going straight to federal court, remote work or paid leave while a claim is pending, and the knowledge that a member who personally harasses or retaliates — not the taxpayer — pays the settlement or award.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the requirement that an employee complete counseling and mediation before filing a claim with the Office of Compliance, and gives the Office's General Counsel power to investigate claims and issue subpoenas on its own [S2][S3][S4].

Requires current and former members to reimburse the Treasury for awards or settlements tied to their own acts of discrimination or retaliation, with the amount withheld from salary after 90 days or taken from their Thrift Savings retirement account after 180 days [S3][S4].
Automatically refers the final disposition of claims against members and senior staff to the House or Senate ethics committees, with access to the underlying records [S3][S4].

Extends nondiscrimination protections to unpaid interns, detailees, and fellows, to Library of Congress employees, and to staff of the China and Helsinki commissions and the Stennis Center, and lets employees request remote work or paid leave while a claim is pending [S3][S4].
Requires the Office to publish semiannual reports listing each award or settlement, the employing office involved, and the amount — without identifying the complaining employee [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, past and present, who would have to repay the Treasury with their own money for settlements connected to their personal conduct, including through payroll withholding and retirement-account transfers. Non-congressional legislative offices that violate the law would also have to reimburse settlement payments out of their operating funds.

drawbacks.text: Claims and investigations remain confidential under the bill, and the public reports cannot name the individual employees involved, so the full picture of misconduct stays partly hidden [S3][S4].

A member accused of personal discrimination gains the right to intervene in the mediation, hearing, or civil action to protect their financial interest, and employees must file claims within 180 days of the violation — limits an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3][S4].

The Office's new authority to recommend that Architect of the Capitol and Capitol Police employees use their offices' own grievance procedures could route some claims back into internal channels [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the employees covered, the benefits are substantial and concrete: faster claims, real investigations, court access, and members personally liable for their own misconduct. The main costs fall on members themselves, which is the point of the bill. The remaining confidentiality rules and the 180-day filing window are genuine limitations, but they do not undo the core reforms.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure the day after introduction, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Gregg Harper introduced the bill on February 5, 2018, and it was referred to three House committees [S1][S6].
The next day, February 6, 2018, the House passed it by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure generally reserved for non-controversial bills [S6].

On February 7, 2018, the Senate received the bill and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, where no further action was recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S6].
The bill drew 38 cosponsors — 16 Democrats and 22 Republicans — and the House passed it the day after introduction with no recorded opposition [S5][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who might otherwise have had to personally repay harassment and discrimination settlements — and legislative branch offices shielded from the bill's transparency and coverage changes — were better off because the Senate never voted. Legislative branch employees lost the reforms for the remainder of that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress, because the Senate never acted

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (16 Democratic and 22 Republican cosponsors) and passed the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition; there is no Senate roll call, since the Senate never voted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have made members personally repay taxpayer-funded harassment and discrimination settlements from their own pay and retirement accounts and would have sent those cases to the ethics committees automatically. Members had an interest in keeping settlements taxpayer-funded and procedures slow.

industries.industry: Legislative branch offices (Architect of the Capitol, Capitol Police, commissions, Library of Congress)
industries.note: The bill would require non-congressional offices to reimburse Treasury for settlement payments and extended workplace-rights coverage to Library of Congress staff and unpaid interns, but it also gave the offices training obligations and, for some employees, an option to keep using internal grievance channels.

industries.industry: Legislative branch employees and unpaid interns
industries.note: These are the workers the bill covers: they would gain faster claim procedures, investigations with subpoena power, court access, and protections against retaliation, including for unpaid interns who previously had none.
